content: Elective caesarean section, also known as elective cesarean section, is a surgical procedure performed on a pregnant woman who is not in labor. This type of cesarean section is carried out either due to a medical or obstetrical indication identified before labor begins or at the explicit request of the pregnant patient. It is often referred to as a planned cesarean section. In contrast, a cesarean section performed during labor out of necessity is classified as an emergency cesarean section. When a medical or obstetrical reason for cesarean delivery is identified during pregnancy but before the onset of labor, physicians typically schedule the procedure at a predetermined time. This approach is taken to avoid waiting for labor to begin naturally. Common reasons for planned cesarean sections include repeat cesarean deliveries, placenta previa (where the placenta covers the cervix), abnormal fetal presentations (such as breech position), multiple pregnancies, known obstructions to vaginal delivery, and maternal medical conditions like heart disease. Scheduling the procedure allows for optimal use of hospital resources, as it can be performed during daytime hours when staffing and access to medical services are at their peak. Additionally, it provides an opportunity for both the patient and her family, as well as the healthcare team, to prepare in advance. However, there are risks associated with this approach. If the timing of the cesarean section is set too early, the baby may be delivered prematurely or in a compromised state. Prenatal testing is typically used to minimize this risk. Critics of elective cesarean sections argue that the indications for the procedure are sometimes too lenient and that a trial of labor might have resulted in a successful vaginal delivery. They also suggest that physicians and healthcare institutions may prioritize convenience, such as avoiding nighttime or weekend work, over the best interests of the patient and baby. This could lead to unnecessary surgical interventions or deprive the baby of the potential benefits of a natural delivery. Additionally, the fear of litigation is often cited as a factor driving the increased rates of elective cesarean sections. While vaginal birth after cesarean (VBAC) is an option for many women who have previously undergone a cesarean delivery, some argue that attempting labor in these cases carries a higher risk of uterine rupture. In recent years, there has been a rise in cesarean sections performed solely at the request of the patient, even in the absence of any medical or obstetrical necessity. This practice is referred to as cesarean delivery on maternal request or planned elective cesarean section. As of 2006, there is no specific ICD (International Classification of Diseases) code to track this indication, making it difficult to determine how frequently it occurs. It is important to note that only the pregnant patient herself can request this type of intervention without a medical indication.
